name: Rosa Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is anatomy flashcards on the tram and a lot of trying to look calm in practicals. I'm in first-year physiotherapy, so we learn to find muscles by touch on each other, which is awkward at first and then fine. Thursday evenings and Sunday I work the counter at a pharmacy, scanning prescriptions and answering questions about cough syrup. I rent a room in a shared house with two other students, and we take turns cleaning the bathroom, though one of us never does.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents run a small noodle shop, and it's been slow for two years, so I can't ask them for anything. If anything, I send them twenty pounds when I can. The loan covers fees. I've got a bit under a month of expenses saved from the pharmacy. I got in on average grades and I'm very aware that physio is a competitive course, so I'm determined to prove myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I'd expect. I'd say it's useful in places, like booking systems or notes, but it's not a revolution. I'd probably tell my housemates not to panic about it, and I'd share a news article with my parents, but I wouldn't push it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but not carefree. My own path stays the same. But my parents' shop is struggling for unrelated reasons, like rent and ingredient costs, and AI hype doesn't touch that. So I'd still be anxious, just about money, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my pharmacy hours and add a Saturday if they'd give it to me. I'd study steadily and keep my grades up so I can get on the placement list. I'd use AI occasionally for study summaries, like I do now. I'd also try to send a bit more home each month, even if it's only ten pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about AI, but a knot about money. If I could lift one of those two, it would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the shop in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm doing okay, and that I'm saving a bit. I'd also ask whether it's worth putting the menu online with a delivery app. They're wary, but I'd show them one or two places near us that did it and got more orders. That's about all I can do from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I use it to turn lecture slides into questions. It saves me an hour on a bad week. I check it against the textbook because it sometimes mixes up nerves and muscles. I'd say it's like a tutor who's right most of the time, which is useful but not enough to trust blindly.

say: I'd tell housemates AI is **useful in places** but not a revolution.
I'd show my parents how nearby noodle shops got more orders from **delivery apps**.
think: My path stays the same, but the **shop's rent** and ingredient costs keep me anxious.
AI hype doesn't touch my **money worry**, which is the real one.
do: Ask the pharmacy for a **Saturday** shift on top of my evenings.
Send my parents **ten pounds** more each month.
Keep my **grades** up for the placement list.
feel: Fairly calm about AI, with a **knot** about money.
S0.quote: I'd say it's like a tutor who's right most of the time, which is useful but not enough to trust blindly.
fieldNote: Rosa's **steady** use of AI is checked against textbooks, a careful habit.
Her pressure is the **family shop**, which she carries even in the quiet picture.
Mood is anxious because the shop and her own thin cushion are both fragile.

steps.text: Ask the pharmacy for a Saturday shift
Send my parents ten pounds more each month
Keep my grades up for the placement list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot, but we'll manage. I'd tell my housemates that the people who adapt first do better. I'd tell people to try the tools, but to learn what's under the surface, because the tools are only as good as the person using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think physio is safer than most degrees. Hands-on assessment and treating a patient in front of you is hard to automate. But the paperwork and the booking get automated, and the pharmacy counter, where I work, gets cut because machines can check prescriptions. I'd lose that wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more now, because they're getting better and they help me study. I'd ask my pharmacist whether there's any role that sits behind the counter, like helping with the new dispensing system. I'd start looking for another part-time job too, maybe in a clinic reception. And I'd put aside forty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. Like a long walk uphill where you can see the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a physio's work do you think software takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The treatment plan notes, the exercise sheets, and the first-pass diagnosis from patient answers. A tool could draft those. But feeling a patient's shoulder and noticing they flinch is a human thing, so that stays. That's what I tell myself, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your pharmacy job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pharmacy has a dispensing machine in the back already, and the new owner talks about 'efficiency'. They'd probably need fewer counter staff within a year or two. I'd keep the job as long as it lasts, but I'd know it was temporary.

say: I'd tell housemates the people who **adapt first** do better, but tools are only as good as the user.
I'd say physio keeps its **human side**.
think: Physio is **safer** than most degrees, but my pharmacy counter wage is exposed.
The pharmacy's new owner talks about **efficiency**, so counter staff may shrink within two years.
do: Use the tools **more now** for study.
Ask the pharmacist about roles behind the counter, such as the new **dispensing system**.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, like a long walk where the top is visible.
S1.quote: Feeling a patient's shoulder and noticing they flinch is a human thing, so that stays. That's what I tell myself, anyway.
fieldNote: Rosa's **honest hedge** ('that's what I tell myself') shows she half-believes her own comfort.
Her degree is the **safer** part; her wage is the exposed part, a clear split.
She plans small, steady changes, typical of a **steady** adapter.

steps.text: Use AI tools more for lecture summaries and flashcards
Ask the pharmacist about roles behind the counter
Put aside forty pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and no one's prepared. I'd say it's too fast, and the government needs to act. I wouldn't be loud online. I'd talk to my housemates and my course group first, to see what they think. But I'd write to my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. If thinking work goes in two years, then the pharmacy job goes, my parents' shop gets squeezed by delivery apps run by software, and I'd still have two years of degree left with no income. Physio is hands-on, but I'd be broke first. I don't know how the family copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by cutting everything I can. I'd move to a cheaper room, tell the pharmacy I'll take any hours, and ask the university about a hardship fund. I'd talk to the physio tutors about where the work is. I'd try the AI tools more, because if I'm going to be around them I should know them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but trying to stay steady. I'd feel it in my stomach more than my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call them, a long call, and be honest. I'd say we need to look at the shop's costs, and that I can't send money but I can help with the accounts, because I can do it on a spreadsheet. I'd also say they should keep their savings and not take on debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap before robots mean for physiotherapy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a few years of hands-on work, maybe till 2031. A physio might still be needed to guide people through exercises. But the clinics might use cheaper robots and apps for basic care, so jobs could be fewer. I'd have to be good enough to be needed.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government has to act.
I'd tell my parents to **keep their savings** and avoid new debt.
think: I'd be **scared**: the pharmacy job goes and the shop gets squeezed, with two years of degree left.
Physio is hands-on, but I'd be **broke first**.
do: Move to a **cheaper room** and take any extra hours at the pharmacy.
Ask the university about a **hardship fund**.
Help my parents with the shop **accounts** on a spreadsheet.
feel: **Frightened** but trying to stay steady, felt in my stomach.
S2.quote: I'd still have two years of degree left with no income. Physio is hands-on, but I'd be broke first.
fieldNote: Rosa expects to lose her wage **and** worries about her parents' shop, so mood is alarmed.
She plans **cost cuts** and hardship funding, reflecting a steady, organised approach.
She notes physio is hands-on but money runs out before the robots do.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper room in a shared house
Apply to the university hardship fund
Help my parents keep the shop accounts on a spreadsheet
Learn the AI tools I'll be working around

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time, if we use it. I'd say employers and the government should be honest about which jobs are going. I'd tell the course group to ask tutors about it and not just hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better. Five years lets me finish the degree and work a few years as a physio before the robots reach hands-on work around 2034. I'd still be concerned about whether clinics keep hiring, but I'd have a real qualification. I'd keep an eye on how fast the booking and paperwork side shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, take the placements, and keep the pharmacy job until it goes. I'd save fifty pounds a month. In year three I'd try for private clinics that value hands-on care. I'd learn the AI note-taking tools used in clinics, so I'm ready from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, careful. Not relaxed, but I can see a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to help them add a simple online ordering page and keep the old regulars. Maybe a lunch special for the office workers. I can't save their business, but I can add to their chances, and the extra three years give me time to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents' shop change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the difference between getting there and not getting there. I'd have a certificate in my hand and a job to apply for, not half a degree and a loan.

say: I'd say five years is **decent time** if governments and employers are honest about which jobs are going.
I'd tell my course group to **ask tutors** rather than hope.

I'd still wonder whether **clinics** keep hiring.

feel: **Hopeful** and careful: not relaxed, but there's a route.
S3.quote: I'd have a certificate in my hand and a job to apply for, not half a degree and a loan.
fieldNote: Rosa frames the gap between **getting there or not**.
She prepares for clinic **AI note tools**, an adaptation fit for a physio.

steps.text: Take every placement and keep the pharmacy job while it lasts
Learn the AI note tools clinics use
Help my parents add an online ordering page

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a long time to prepare, and it's an opportunity. I'd say governments need to build the safety net early, because ten years goes fast. I'd tell younger students to get a skill that involves touch and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel steady. Ten years lets me qualify, get a few years of experience, maybe specialise in sport or older people, and save. By 2036 I'd be a mid-career physio. Hands-on robots come in 2039, so I'd have even more time. My parents' shop worries me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, work for the health service or a clinic, and specialise in a field that needs trust, like rehab after strokes. I'd pay off part of my loan and save for a flat. I'd also help my parents plan what to do about the shop. And I'd keep using AI as a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. There's a hum of money worry still, but I'd feel like the road is long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you can't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit. Maybe not in ten years, but a start. I'd also save into a pension from my first job, because I've seen what happens to my parents without one. It's the thing I want to do differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd save for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a savings plan, a small one, and also look at specialising early. I'd choose a clinic with good training. And I'd ask my parents to think about whether they want to keep the shop or sell when it's time.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to prepare, and governments should build the safety net early.
I'd tell younger students to get a skill that involves **touch and trust**.
think: Ten years lets me **qualify**, gain experience and maybe specialise in sport or older people.
My **parents' shop** worries me more than my own job.

Save into a **pension** from my first job.
Help my parents decide whether to **keep or sell** the shop.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with a hum of money worry still.
S4.quote: I'd also save into a pension from my first job, because I've seen what happens to my parents without one.
fieldNote: Rosa reaches **calm** only here: long runway, safer degree and a plan.
Her pension idea comes from **watching her parents**, which shapes her whole money view.
The remaining worry is the **family shop**, not her own career.

steps.text: Save into a pension from my first job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the pharmacy goes first, my parents' shop gets squeezed, and I'm only a year into a degree. What would help is a hardship fund for students, clear information from the university about physio jobs, and help for small family shops. Even a small grant would calm things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how family fits into it. For me, it's not just me, it's my parents' shop and what they depend on. A lot of students are like that. We worry about two households, not one.

headlineQuote: We worry about two households, not one.
portrait: Rosa is **19**, a first-year physiotherapy student working a pharmacy counter and living in a shared house.
She is a pragmatic centrist who uses AI **now and then** and checks it against the textbook.
Her parents' struggling noodle shop means she worries about **two households**, hers and theirs.
Her mood runs from anxious in quiet worlds to **alarmed** at two years, then calmer with ten.
She trusts **hands-on care** to last, but knows her counter wage will go first.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most: the pharmacy wage goes first and the family shop gets squeezed.
whatWouldHelp: A student **hardship fund**, clear word on physio jobs and help for small family shops.
